details:
**John Stuart Mill**
The English philosopher who wrote On Liberty, published in 1859. Mill is also the author of Utilitarianism and The Subjection of Women, and he dedicated On Liberty to his late wife, Harriet Taylor.

**Harm principle**
The work's central idea. The only legitimate reason for society or the state to use power over an individual against their will is to prevent harm to others; a person's own good, physical or moral, is not enough reason.

**"Tyranny of the majority"**
Mill warns in Chapter I that in popular governments the majority can oppress individuals, not only through laws but through the pressure of public opinion and custom. He borrowed the phrase from Alexis de Tocqueville's Democracy in America.

**"Of Individuality, as One of the Elements of Well-Being"**
The title of Chapter III. Mill argues that people should be free to develop their own characters and "experiments of living," and he praises "individuality of power and development."

**Assumption of infallibility**
In Chapter II, on liberty of thought and discussion, Mill argues that silencing any opinion assumes that we cannot be wrong. Since we can be wrong, a silenced opinion might be true, and even false opinions help keep true beliefs alive and understood.

**Truth does not always triumph over persecution**
Mill rejects the comforting idea that truth always wins out against persecution in the end. He argues that history shows persecution has often succeeded in stamping out true ideas, so free discussion must be actively protected.

**Ban on eating pork**
In Chapter IV, Mill imagines Muslims (he writes "Mahomedans") forming a majority in a country and banning pork. He uses the example to show that the majority's disgust or religious feelings do not justify interfering with people's private conduct.

**"An Akbar or a Charlemagne"**
Mill limits his principles to mature, "civilized" societies. He says that "barbarians" who are not yet capable of improving themselves through free discussion can only hope for obedience to a ruler like the Mughal emperor Akbar or the Frankish king Charlemagne.

**The unsafe bridge**
Mill's example of when interference is allowed. If a public official sees someone about to cross a bridge known to be unsafe, and there is no time to warn him, the official may seize him and turn him back, because no one truly wants to fall into the river.

**"A state which dwarfs its men"**
From the work's closing paragraph: "a State which dwarfs its men, in order that they may be more docile instruments in its hands even for beneficial purposes, will find that with small men no great thing can really be accomplished." Mill warns against government that stifles individual development.

**Wilhelm von Humboldt**
The Prussian thinker whose work The Limits of State Action influenced Mill. On Liberty opens with an epigraph from Humboldt about the importance of human development in its richest diversity, and helped introduce his ideas to English readers.

**Liberty and the social contract**
Questions on liberty in general also mention Jean-Jacques Rousseau, whose The Social Contract opens with "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." In the same work, Rousseau quotes the Latin saying that he prefers dangerous liberty to peaceful slavery.
